title: Mexican Book Fairs
author: Elena Poniatowska
content:
_This article by[Elena
Poniatowska](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Elena%20Poniatowska)
originally appeared in the [October 11, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/11/opinion/ferias-del-
libro-mexicanas-elena-poniatowska), Mexico's premier left wing daily
newspaper._

On October 9, the 26th edition of the Zócalo International Book Fair (FIL del
Zócalo) opened, coordinated by Paloma Saiz Tejero, a tireless cultural
promoter and lover of reading. For two weeks, the Zócalo of Mexico City is the
meeting point for children, young people, and grandparents who pack the wide
aisles where books are lined up as in a market of lettuces, strawberries, and
limes, because, after all, there are books we devour and others we have no
appetite for, like spinach. The famous publishing houses and the writers who
travel from Spain are offered like fabada and paella next to beans and brain
tacos, pancita, and the black mole of Oaxaca. They display their temptations
because Paloma Saiz and Paco Ignacio Taibo II make books accessible to every
wallet, and many students leave happy because they managed to buy some coveted
volume. **A book is not a luxury** , and more than 350 publishing imprints
display on their tables the works of much-loved authors, such as Juan Rulfo or
Rosario Castellanos, who this year put all of Chiapas in the spotlight.

In its beginnings, the FIL del Zócalo faced the doubts of the publishing
industry. Since 2000, this celebration has been the meeting point of readers
with authors who smile kindly as they autograph their work and tell of their
long journey to Mexico. To this day, the Zócalo is the starting point for
other fairs that seek to win over young readers.

The first book fair in history was Frankfurt's, in 1949, a reference point for
publishers and booksellers, and a showcase for authors who seek to sail on the
Seine or the Thames.

In Mexico, the Guadalajara International Book Fair (FIL) turns 40 this 2026,
thanks to the remarkable work of Raúl Padilla –to whom Carlos Monsiváis and I
will always be grateful for his attentions when we fell ill from so many
letters–, begun in October 1987 and considered as preposterous as setting up a
travel agency in the Lecumberri prison.

Thinking of international pretensions was as illusory as throwing oneself into
the ocean without a life preserver. At most, two or three absent-minded
booksellers and a handful of homegrown writers hungry for the spotlight would
attend.

Today, **the fair receives more than 900,000 visitors** , and the publishers'
pavilions are sailing ships that row from the Old Continent to Mexico.

I remember with emotion that during the 2014 FIL Guadalajara, every hour one
could hear in the aisles of the immense facilities and book stands: "one, two,
three, four, five…" up to 43, to remember **the 43 students of the Ayotzinapa
teachers ' college disappeared on September 26, 2014**. It was also moving to
hear the poem by David Huerta that was repeated like a gospel among the
visitors.

The 2026 Guadalajara gathering has Italy as its guest, in addition to awarding
the FIL Prize for Literature in Romance Languages to Gioconda Belli, the
lovely Nicaraguan, and my admired José Luis Martínez receives the Fernando
Benítez National Homage to Cultural Journalism.

Just like the Guadalajara FIL, the one held in the Zócalo is **an open space
for denunciation, criticism, and protest**. Starting with the names of its
forums dedicated to persecuted writers: Federico García Lorca, Spanish poet
shot by firing squad in August 1936; Alaíde Foppa, disappeared by the
Guatemalan government in 1980; Rodolfo Walsh, the Argentine disappeared in
1977, and José Revueltas, a political persecutee, imprisoned four times
because of his activism, who in the Lecumberri prison wrote _El apando_ ,
adapted for film in 1976 by Felipe Cazals.

In this edition, speakers and authors from Brazil, Colombia, Spain, Argentina,
Chile, and Guatemala are taking part. The FIL will have more than 250
activities, including lectures, book presentations, and concerts.

Within Mexico City, a cosmopolitan capital, several boroughs seek to
strengthen their identity and have set out to promote their own book fairs.
Coyoacán's, with its four editions, has grown remarkably, led by its director,
the young Gerardo Valenzuela. Tláhuac and Azcapotzalco are making their way
with lectures and presentations. The International Children's and Youth Book
Fair, at the National Center for the Arts, unique of its kind, is the most
eagerly awaited by children and young people, from November 12 to 22.

The Monterrey FIL was born thanks to a student initiative, in 1989, with a
single tent in the parking lot of the Tec de Monterrey; it too has established
itself in the publishing world. This year it will feature the participation of
Nobel Prize in Literature laureate Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio and Emmanuel
Carrère. El Colegio Nacional is the guest of honor, as is Juan Villoro,
recently awarded the 2026 Carlos Fuentes International Prize for Literary
Creation in the Spanish Language. From October 10 to 18, authors, scientists,
artists, journalists, researchers, teachers, and readers will walk its aisles.

In Mexico, the Oaxaca Book Fair stands out, from October 12 to 20. Next year
we eagerly await the FIL of the Palacio de Minería in the Historic Center of
Mexico City, next to the Sanborns de los Azulejos, from February 26 to March
7, 2027, as well as the Yucatán International Reading Fair, from March 13 to
21, in which the Yucatecan researcher and writer Sara Poot-Herrera takes part;
she directs the UC-Mexicanistas association, which has a strong presence in
cultural activities.

Although the most recognized international book fairs in Mexico are
practically 10, it is a fact that **around 137 are held in our country** ,
among state, municipal, and university fairs, such as those organized by the
National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), the Book and Rose Fair (April
23), which bursts with literary flowers at the University Cultural Center,
neighbor to the Juan Ruiz de Alarcón theater and the Nezahualcóyotl hall,
where lectures, concerts, and dramatized readings are held.

At the National Library of Mexico, another of the spaces of Ciudad
Universitaria, the second Book and Publishers Fair in Indigenous Languages was
recently organized, which represents a triumph that makes known the literature
of our authors who speak one of the 63 original languages of the national
territory.

The UNAM Institute of Bibliographic Research reported on its social media that
activities were held in the central courtyard of the venue and lectures in the
José María Vigil auditorium to discuss the linguistic and cultural diversity
of Mexico. The purpose of the fair is to disseminate "projects linked to the
production, circulation, and promotion of books in Indigenous languages."

The publications presented are a beautiful mosaic of covers designed with
images of textiles and embroidery, pre-Hispanic ceramics, photographs of women
weaving on backstrap looms, illustrations with children's drawings, and other
graphic expressions of popular art.

Another fair worth mentioning is the International Jewish Book Fair, organized
by the Jewish Documentation and Research Center of Mexico in Mexico City,
which is supported by the Fondo de Cultura Económica, mainly through its
Rosario Castellanos bookstore, in the Condesa neighborhood.

In each edition, the Jewish community shares with us, through book
presentations, lectures, round tables, workshops, and concerts, its memory and
the works of Jewish writers who have dedicated part of their writing to
Mexico, such as Rosa Nissán, author of the novel _Novia que te vea_ , brought
to film by director Guita Shifter in 1991.

Book fairs in Mexico are among the great gatherings that speak of how a people
nourishes itself on books, and they show the joint effort of cultural
institutions, universities, publishers, bookstores, and cultural centers that
each year receive thousands of readers, writers, students, tourists,
academics, researchers, translators, teachers, and boys and girls in search of
the book that will nourish and make happier the hours of their lives.
